title: Winning the Battle of Life (Kurukshetra Within Me) - Part I | Swami Smaranananda Giri

# Winning the Battle of Life: The Kurukshetra Within

### Introduction: The Eternal Conflict

In the teachings of Paramahansa Yogananda, life is never portrayed as a passive journey, but as an active, sacred battlefield. As we open the pages of the Bhagavad Gita, we are not reading about a historical skirmish on the plains of Kurukshetra; we are reading the blueprint of our own consciousness. Swami Smaranananda Giri explores how this internal Kurukshetra represents the perennial struggle between our lower nature—the sensory-driven, ego-identified self—and our higher, divine nature, the Atman.

### The Nature of the Battlefield

Each day, we wake up to a world of dualities. We face desires, fears, attachments, and the constant pull of the senses. This is the Dhritarashtra mentality—the blind mind—that refuses to acknowledge the divinity already present within. The Pandavas, the five sons of Pandu, represent the spiritualized senses and faculties of the soul, while the Kauravas represent the negative habits and unruly desires that seek to usurp our inner kingdom.

**Story • The Architect of One’s Own Destiny**

Story: There once lived a master carpenter who was known for building the most beautiful, intricate houses in the kingdom. As he reached old age, he decided it was time to retire. He went to his employer and asked to be released from his duties. The employer, though saddened, agreed but asked him for one final favor: to build one last house before he left. The carpenter, his mind already on retirement, agreed begrudgingly. He rushed the work, using poor materials and cutting corners at every turn. When he finished, the employer came to inspect the house. He handed the keys to the carpenter and said, "This house is my gift to you for your years of service." The carpenter was shocked. Had he known he was building his own home, he would have done it with the utmost care and precision. We are all master carpenters, building our future lives with our present thoughts and actions. Every decision is a brick in the house we will have to inhabit.

### Understanding the Ego

Winning the battle of life requires a profound shift in perspective. We often identify with the "little self," the ego that craves validation, comfort, and control. This ego is the primary source of all our inner friction. Swami Smaranananda Giri emphasizes that as long as we view ourselves as separate, we remain caught in the cycle of struggle. True victory comes only when we surrender the ego into the Divine, realizing that the warrior fighting the battle is not the human personality, but the soul acting as an instrument of God.

### Practical Steps for Spiritual Victory

1. **Deep Meditation**: Without the internal recharging of Kriya Yoga or the Hong-Sau technique, we enter the battlefield depleted. Meditation provides the armor of spiritual equanimity.
2. **Right Attitude**: We must practice "doing, yet not doing." Perform your duties with intensity, but release the attachment to the results.
3. **Discriminative Intelligence (Buddhi)**: The Kauravas thrive on our lack of awareness. By developing clear, intuitive intelligence, we can spot the seeds of negative habit before they grow into monsters.

### Conclusion: The Divine Charioteer

Ultimately, we cannot win this battle alone. Like Arjuna, we must hand over the reins of our chariot—our body, mind, and senses—to the Divine Charioteer, Lord Krishna. When we invite the Guru into our inner Kurukshetra, the battle changes. It ceases to be a struggle and becomes a leela, a divine sport where the outcome is already secured by the grace of the Supreme.
